meta.title: BBR congestion control: modeling the pipe instead of waiting for loss (v1 → v3)
meta.subject: Computer science
meta.topic: BBR: BtlBw/RTprop model, pacing-gain state machine, v2/v3 loss + ECN bounds, coexistence with CUBIC

story.title: Send at the pipe's size and the queue stays near empty

tldr: BBR estimates the path's bottleneck bandwidth (BtlBw) and propagation delay (RTprop), then paces packets at the rate the bottleneck drains, so the queue stays near empty. It probes up 25% and back down, and re-measures RTprop every few seconds. v1 ignored loss; v3 bounds loss at 2% per round and is what Google runs on public traffic.
why: Why it matters: loss-based CUBIC fills deep buffers and adds hundreds of ms of delay, while BBR keeps the queue near one BDP. Google runs v3 on public traffic and Linux mainline ships v1, so its fairness with CUBIC matters now.

stats.l: BBR's fixed share vs CUBIC (Ware et al. 2019)

cards.title: Send at the booth's speed and the parking lot stays nearly empty
cards.brief:
Cars queue at a toll booth whenever they arrive too fast. BBR watches how fast cars leave the booth and how short the empty-lot trip is, then sends at the matching pace so the lot stays nearly empty.

Same 12 Mbit/s, but the café ping stays near 55 ms instead of 220 ms.

cards.title: Six terms cover the whole algorithm
cards.brief:
• cwnd: cap on unacknowledged bytes in flight.
  • Loss-based CC: grow until a drop, then cut (×0.5 Reno, ×0.7 CUBIC).
  • BDP: rate × RTT, the bytes needed to fill the pipe.
  • Bufferbloat: oversized buffers that loss-based CC fills.
  • Pacing: spacing packets at a target rate.
  • ECN: routers mark instead of drop.

cards.title: Google and YouTube run it, Linux ships it, one sysctl away
cards.brief: Google's B4 WAN and YouTube run BBRv3, Linux mainline still ships BBRv1 (since 4.9), and AWS CloudFront saw up to 22% more aggregate throughput. Operators switch it on with tcp_congestion_control=bbr and read live state with ss -tin.

cards.title: The one-liner hides five traps, starting with a measurement conflict
cards.brief: "Measure bandwidth and min RTT, then pace" hides five things: you cannot see both at once, gains above and below 1 are required, cwnd still sets the share against CUBIC, v1 ignored loss, and jitter breaks the model.

cards.title: Loss-based CC fills the buffer, BBR aims for the knee
cards.brief:
Every path has a bottleneck rate (BtlBw) and a propagation RTT (RTprop). Loss-based CC rides the full-buffer edge. The optimum is the knee at BDP. In the toy sim, Reno's median RTT is 221 ms and BBR's is 55.5 ms at the same goodput.

Interactive Kleinrock slider inside.

cards.title: Two gauges on one hose: peak flow and fastest transit
cards.brief: A garden hose of unknown width and length: an outflow meter gives the diameter (BtlBw), a dye timer gives the length (RTprop). Set the tap to their product, probe a little wider, then ease off to drain the puddle. The analogy breaks on shared hoses, bursty ACKs and policers.

cards.title: Startup overshoots, drain repairs, then probe and pay back
cards.brief:
Startup grows the send rate by gain 2.77 per round and overshoots to ~72 packets of queue before the plateau near 12 Mbit/s. Drain empties it. ProbeBW then cruises at gain 1.0 and alternates 1.25 and 0.75, so the average gain is 1.0.

8-step walkthrough and state machine inside.

cards.title: The filters converge from one side, and the gains average to 1
cards.brief:
Min RTT converges to R from above and max bandwidth to B from below, so each filter is biased only toward the truth. Startup gain is 4 ln 2 ≈ 2.77. Against 1% loss, BBR must probe within about 137 rounds, which is why v3 picks 62–63.

Shares plot inside.

cards.title: Two filters on two timescales, with pacing as the control
cards.brief: Bandwidth changes with competition, so it gets a short max window. Propagation delay changes with routing, so it gets a long min window. Pacing sets the rate. Remove the 1.25 probe and BBR never finds new capacity. Remove ProbeRTT and a route change goes unnoticed.

cards.title: Probe timers and gains trade speed for fairness
cards.brief:
v3 raises the DOWN gain from 0.75 to 0.9 and bounds loss at 2% per round. Alternatives: CUBIC + HyStart++ for the default, Copa and Vegas for low queues that lose to buffer-fillers, learned controllers, and L4S, which moves the signal into the network.

Per-CCA fairness plot inside.

cards.title: BBR is not delay-based, and its failures are fairness failures
cards.brief:
Shallow buffers cost v1 324 drops against Reno's 8 in the sim. BBR takes a fixed ~40% against CUBIC. RTT unfairness persists in v3. With ECN on, one BBRv3 flow took ~99% against five CUBIC flows.

Queue-trace figure inside.

cards.title: Shipped BBR is v3 at Google and v1 in mainline Linux
cards.brief:
Google's public traffic runs v3, while Linux mainline still ships v1. Inside datacenters BBR.Swift replaces it. QUIC stacks run BBR in user space, where timer accuracy matters. Verizon saw a ~50% regression on PoP-to-PoP links and kept CUBIC there.

BBRv3 queue traces inside.

cards.title: v3 kept the CUBIC unfairness, and the fixes are still open
cards.brief:
Independent 2024–2026 studies found v3 keeps v1's unfairness to CUBIC, and ECN makes it worse. A 2025 IFIP study says no model fits v3 yet. FRCC (NSDI 2026) aims for provable starvation-freedom, and the IETF is standardizing v3 as an Experimental draft.

Remedy comparison inside.

cards.title: Fair share, jitter and a model of v3 remain unsolved
cards.brief: Four questions have no accepted answer: what "fair" means between different CCAs (Jain's index or harm?), coexistence with CUBIC in shallow buffers, delay signals that survive jitter without losing low delay, and an analytical model of v3.

cards.title: From Kleinrock's 1979 power metric to the 2026 IETF draft
cards.brief: Kleinrock set the optimum at BDP in 1979. Jacobson's ACK clock (1988) and CUBIC (2008) followed. BBRv1 shipped in 2016, BBRv3 in 2023, and BBR became an IETF working-group draft (draft-ietf-ccwg-bbr-06) in 2026.

cards.title: Drag the buffer: Reno's delay follows it, BBR's does not
cards.brief:
Run the toy simulator and move the buffer. Reno's RTT tracks it (221 → 670 ms) while BBR stays near 55 ms. At 0.5 BDP, the BBRv1-like sender drops 324 packets against Reno's 8, for 5% more goodput.

Interactive Reno vs BBR simulator inside.

cards.title: Core papers, the IETF draft and the v3 measurement studies
cards.brief: The 2016 ACM Queue paper, draft-ietf-ccwg-bbr-06, Ware et al. (IMC 2019), Arun et al. (SIGCOMM 2022), the 2024–2026 v3 studies, and Google's and Linux's code.

cold.q: Reno's median round trip in the toy sim, on a link whose empty round trip is 40 ms?
cold.reveal: 221 ms. Reno's median round trip in the toy sim, with an 8×BDP buffer. The same link with BBR gives 55.5 ms, close to the empty 40 ms.

gain.q: During Startup, BBR raises the sending rate by one fixed pacing gain each round. What is it?
gain.reveal: 2.77, which is 4 ln 2. Older BBRv1 used 2/ln 2 = 2.885. The rate grows about 2.8× per round until the pipe looks full.

rounds.q: Against 1% random loss, how many rounds can BBR wait between probes and still hold its rate?
rounds.reveal: About 137 rounds, from the math section: BBR can wait up to ~137 rounds between probes and still tolerate 1% random loss. That is why BBRv3 picks 62–63 rounds.

drops.q: In the toy sim with a shallow buffer, which sender drops more packets, and by how much?
drops.reveal: BBRv1, about 40×. The sim shows 324 drops for BBRv1 against 8 for Reno. BBRv1 ignores loss, so it keeps pacing into a buffer that is too small.

questions.q: When an ACK arrives, exactly which two intervals does BBR compare to compute a delivery-rate sample, and why the max of the two?
questions.a: send_elapsed = P.sent_time − P.first_sent_time (how long the sender took to send the flight) and ack_elapsed = now − P.delivered_time (how long the ACKs for it took to come back). The rate is Δdelivered / max(send_elapsed, ack_elapsed). ACK compression or aggregation can make ack_elapsed artificially short, and a sender burst can make send_elapsed short. The bottleneck can't deliver faster than either one, so the larger interval gives the conservative, unbiased-low estimate.

questions.q: What happens to max_bw when the application goes idle for 2 s, then resumes?
questions.a: During idle, any samples are marked app-limited and can't lower max_bw. If the idle lasts longer than the filter window (10 rounds in v1), the old peak expires only when it is replaced. Implementations keep the last max because app-limited samples are ignored unless they're higher. On restart BBR paces at the old max_bw, not slow-start. Linux also has a "restart from idle" path that paces at pacing_gain=1·bw so it doesn't dump a burst.

questions.q: Walk through what ProbeBW_UP does in v3 if loss reaches 3% halfway through the phase.
questions.a: The loss rate for the round crosses LossThresh = 2%. BBR sets inflight_longterm to the inflight at which loss crossed the threshold (with a correction to estimate where it crossed 2%), sets prev_probe_too_high, exits UP to DOWN, and cuts the short-term bounds by β = 0.7. The next UP is a short "precautionary" probe until it shows no excess loss.

questions.q: Why does ProbeRTT trigger on "min_rtt not refreshed" rather than on a fixed timer?
questions.a: If the flow naturally observed a new minimum (for example, the app was idle and the queue emptied, or another flow left), there's no need to dip. Triggering only when min_rtt hasn't been refreshed for ProbeRTTInterval (5 s in v3) avoids the throughput cost for flows that see the true RTprop for free. It also tends to synchronize competing BBR flows: they all see the same queue, so they all go stale and dip together, and that dip empties the queue for everyone.

questions.q: Why is the Startup gain ~2.77–2.89 and not 2?
questions.a: The bandwidth estimate lags: it's the delivery rate of data sent about a round ago, averaged over a round, and reported a round later. For the send rate to double each round, the gain must correct for that lag. Integrating an exponential r₀2^{t/R} over [t−2R, t−R] gives r(t)/(4 ln 2), so g = 4 ln 2 ≈ 2.77. Gain 2 would grow more slowly than 2× per round, roughly 1.4–1.5×, and take many more rounds to find BtlBw.

questions.q: Why does BBR need a cwnd at all if it paces?
questions.a: Pacing is open-loop between ACKs. If the path stalls (ACK loss, a delay spike, ACK aggregation gaps) a pure pacer keeps sending at max_bw with no feedback. cwnd = 2·BDP bounds inflight so that a stall costs at most one extra BDP of queue. Against CUBIC, that cap is what sets BBRv1's share.

questions.q: Why does v3 use 0.9 in DOWN instead of v1's 0.75?
questions.a: The draft calls 0.9 "the minimum pacing_gain that allows bandwidth-based convergence to approximate fairness", given UP = 1.25. It also gives up less throughput during DOWN. v3 no longer depends on DOWN to empty the queue fully. It uses inflight bounds and Headroom (CRUISE at 0.85 × inflight_longterm) to keep queues low.

questions.q: Why 62–63 rounds for T_reno and not, say, 200?
questions.a: Two constraints. With much fewer than ~60 rounds between probes (each probe may cause loss), Reno/CUBIC flows can't regrow enough to carry 4K video. With too many rounds, BBR can't tolerate 1% random loss: (0.99)^N · 4 ≥ 1 requires N ≤ ~137. 62–63 satisfies both, and the randomization avoids synchronization.

questions.q: If you made the RTprop filter 60 s instead of 10 s, what breaks?
questions.a: ProbeRTT would happen much less often (good for throughput), but a route change that raises propagation delay would go unnoticed for up to 60 s. BDP would be underestimated and BBR would be cwnd-limited below capacity. Competing BBR flows would also stay on standing-queue-inflated estimates longer, and multi-flow queue drains would be rarer.

questions.q: If cwnd_gain were 1 instead of 2, what would happen on a Wi-Fi link with ACK aggregation?
questions.a: ACKs arrive in clumps separated by gaps. With cwnd = 1·BDP, the sender exhausts cwnd during a gap and idles until the next clump, so throughput drops well below BtlBw. That is exactly the problem behind the Wi-Fi patches. Gain 2 plus extra_acked gives enough headroom to keep sending through gaps.

questions.q: What if every flow on the Internet ran BBRv1, so there is no CUBIC at all? Does bufferbloat vanish?
questions.a: The standing queue would mostly vanish: each flow paces near its share and probes ±25%. But not entirely. Multiple v1 flows each overestimate their share by a bit, and studies found BBR-vs-BBR queues of about 1–2 BDP in deep buffers, plus RTT unfairness and massive loss in shallow buffers. v2/v3 bounds fix much of that.

questions.q: How could an on-path middlebox make a BBR sender wildly overestimate bandwidth?
questions.a: Hold ACKs and release them in a burst (ACK compression or aggregation) so a short ack_elapsed interval inflates samples. Or ACK data optimistically before it is delivered (a split-TCP or ACK-spoofing proxy). max(send_elapsed, ack_elapsed) and extra_acked bound but don't eliminate the first. The second fools every CC.

questions.q: Construct a scenario where two BBR flows on the same bottleneck get a 10:1 split.
questions.a: Give the flows very different RTprops on a deep-buffer bottleneck: say 10 ms vs 200 ms. Each caps inflight at 2·its own BDP. The long-RTT flow's cap is 20× larger, so it holds most of the queue, and its delivery rate wins in the max filter. PAM 2024 reports this persists in v3. Alternatively, add non-congestive jitter > 2× the equilibrium delay oscillation to one flow's path (the starvation construction).

questions.q: Why does enabling ECN on a classic-AQM router make BBRv3 more unfair to CUBIC?
questions.a: v3 reacts to CE like DCTCP: proportionally to the fraction marked. CUBIC reacts to any CE like a loss, so it cuts its window by 30%. A classic AQM marks well before dropping, so CUBIC keeps backing off on marks while v3 trims only a little. Zeynali et al. (ANRW 2024) measured one v3 flow taking >~99% vs five CUBIC flows with ECN on.

questions.q: How does BBR's delivery-rate estimator relate to TCP's ACK clock from Jacobson '88?
questions.a: Jacobson's ACK clock says ACK arrivals are paced by the bottleneck, so sending one packet per ACK self-clocks to the bottleneck rate. BBR measures that clock explicitly (Δdelivered/Δt), filters it with a max, and replaces ACK-clocked sending with timer-driven pacing at that rate. That's why it survives ACK compression better than pure ACK clocking.

questions.q: How is BBR's "probe up, pay back" related to CUBIC's concave/convex window curve around W_max?
questions.a: CUBIC grows concavely toward the last W_max (cautious near the known ceiling), then convexly beyond it (probing for more). v3's CRUISE at 85% of inflight_longterm then REFILL/UP is the same "stay below the known-safe ceiling, then periodically probe above it" idea, with the ceiling learned from loss/ECN rather than from the last drop.

questions.q: How does L4S change the problem BBR is trying to solve?
questions.a: L4S AQMs mark CE at a very shallow queue threshold with a scalable signal and isolate L4S traffic in its own queue. The sender no longer needs to infer the queue from RTT or probe for bandwidth by overshooting. The network tells it. The BBR question becomes "how to respond to a scalable ECN signal while sharing with non-L4S flows", and that is why v3 adopted DCTCP-style ECN.

questions.q: Can any sender-only CCA be both starvation-free under jitter and low-delay?
questions.a: Unsettled. Arun et al. show delay-convergent CCAs must oscillate by at least half the jitter to avoid starvation, which means some delay floor. FRCC (NSDI 2026) claims provable fairness under jitter by separating flow-count estimation from capacity estimation. Whether that also gives low delay on real Internet paths, and how it coexists with CUBIC, is open.

questions.q: What fairness metric should the IETF use to judge whether BBRv3 is "safe to deploy"?
questions.a: Candidates: Jain's index (simple, ignores duration and harm), max-min fairness (needs to know demand), and "harm" (Ware et al. 2019: compare a flow's performance with and without the newcomer, so it's acceptable if you harm others no more than CUBIC harms them). The IETF hasn't standardized one. BBRv3 is on the Experimental track partly for this reason.
